nt: Since people strike their palms together in order to applaud, it may be more natural in your language to use a plural term here. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [Clap your hands]

It might seem that to say both **Shout** and **voice** would be to express extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can use just one of these terms in your translation. Alternate translation: [Celebrate by shouting to God] or [Lift your voice to God in rejoicing]

This verse gives the reason for the result that the previous verse describes. See the discussion in the introduction to this psalm of how you might order the reason and result here and in verses 6 and 7.
יְהוָ֣ה עֶלְי֣וֹן נוֹרָ֑א מֶ֥לֶךְ גָּ֝דוֹל עַל־כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that Yahweh is **the great king over all of the earth** with the information that he is **the Most High**. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the Most High, the great king over all of the earth, is to be feared]

The expression **is to be feared** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People should fear Yahweh, the Most High]

x.ASV: He subdueth peoples under us, And nations under our feet.
x.Darby: He subdueth the peoples under us, and the nations under our feet.
x.KJV: He shall subdue the people under us, and the nations under our feet.
x.YLT: He leadeth peoples under us, and nations under our feet.

nt: יַדְבֵּ֣ר עַמִּ֣ים תַּחְתֵּ֑י⁠נוּ וּ֝⁠לְאֻמִּ֗ים תַּ֣חַת רַגְלֵֽי⁠נוּ

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. It may be clearer in your language to connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Another approach would be to combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [He has subdued peoples under us, yes, he has subdued nations under our feet] or [He has subdued many nations under our feet]
יַדְבֵּ֣ר עַמִּ֣ים תַּחְתֵּ֑י⁠נוּ וּ֝⁠לְאֻמִּ֗ים תַּ֣חַת רַגְלֵֽי⁠נוּ

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh actually put **peoples** and **nations** **under** the **feet** of the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He has enabled us to defeat peoples, yes, he has enabled us to defeat nations] or [He has enabled us to defeat many nations]

nt: The psalmist is speaking as if the land of Canaan were something that the Israelites had inherited as a lasting possession. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the land that would be our lasting possession]

The psalmist is using **Jacob** to represent his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the pride of the descendants of Jacob, whom he loved]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [of which the descendants of Jacob, whom he loved, are proud]
See how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent the term **Selah**.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh our God has gone up with a shout and the sound of a shofar]
עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּ⁠תְרוּעָ֑ה יְ֝הֹוָ֗ה בְּ⁠ק֣וֹל שׁוֹפָֽר

The psalmist is using the expression **gone up** to mean that God has ascended onto his throne as king. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [God has ascended his throne with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a shofar] or [Yahweh our God has ascended his throne with a shout and the sound of a shofar]
עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּ⁠תְרוּעָ֑ה יְ֝הֹוָ֗ה בְּ⁠ק֣וֹל שׁוֹפָֽר

The psalmist is using God going up onto his throne to represent him assuming the role of king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [God has become king with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a shofar] or [Yahweh our God has become king with a shout and the sound of a shofar]
עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּ⁠תְרוּעָ֑ה יְ֝הֹוָ֗ה בְּ⁠ק֣וֹל שׁוֹפָֽר

As passages such as [2 Samuel 15:10](../2sa/15/10.md) and [2 Kings 9:13](../2ki/09/13.md) illustrate, shouting that a person was the king and blowing a shofar were symbolic actions by which people acclaimed that person as their new king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. The UST models one way to do that.

In each part of this verse, the psalmist is repeating the expression “sing praise” in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat expressions for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Sing praise to God enthusiastically! Yes, sing praise to our king enthusiastically!]

x.Darby: ForGod is the King of all the earth; sing psalms with understanding.
x.KJV: For God is the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding.
x.YLT: For king of all the earth is God, Give praise, O understanding one.

nt: The psalmist is using a musical term here, **maskil**, that also occurs in the superscriptions to several psalms. Biblical scholars have different understandings of what this term means. (See the discussion in the introduction to the book of Psalms.) Since the meaning is not certain, in your translation, you may wish to represent this word in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language, as the ULT does. You could also use a general expression, as the UST does.

x.ASV: God reigneth over the nations: God sitteth upon his holy throne.
x.Darby: God reigneth over the nations;God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness.
x.KJV: God reigneth over the heathen: God sitteth upon the throne of his holiness.
x.YLT: God hath reigned over nations, God hath sat on His holy throne,

nt: Since the psalmist has already used the name **God** earlier in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. (However, the repetition of the name has a poetic effect, so you may wish to repeat the name in your own translation.) Alternate translation: [he sits on the throne of his holiness]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **throne**, representing God’s reign, that is characterized by **holiness**. The idea is that God’s reign is not common, that is, it is not like the usual reign of kings on earth, who are not always just in their dealings with their people. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God reigns with perfect justice] or [he reigns with perfect justice]

x.ASV: The princes of the peoples are gathered together To be the people of the God of Abraham; For the shields of the earth belong unto God: He is greatly exalted.
x.Darby: The willing-hearted of the peoples have gathered together, [with] the people of theGod of Abraham. For untoGod [belong] the shields of the earth: he is greatly exalted.
x.KJV: The princes of the people are gathered together, even the people of the God of Abraham: for the shields of the earth belong unto God: he is greatly exalted.
x.YLT: Nobles of peoples have been gathered, With the people of the God of Abraham, For to God are the shields of earth, Greatly hath He been exalted!

nt: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before as modeled in the UST.

Here, **shields** represents “rulers,” since rulers are protectors. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the rulers of the earth belong to God] or [God reigns over the rulers of the earth]

The expression **is greatly exalted** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. This could mean: (1) that God has exalted himself. Alternate translation: [He has exalted himself greatly] or (2) that people should or do exalt God. Alternate translation: [People should exalt him greatly] or [People exalt him greatly]
